questions.stem: Article 19 of the Constitution originally enumerated SEVEN freedoms. The 'right to acquire, hold and dispose of property' [Article 19(1)(f)] was DELETED by which Constitutional Amendment, thereby reducing the freedoms to the current SIX?
questions.explanation: The 44th Amendment Act 1978 — passed by the Janata Government after the 1977 elections — deleted Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31 (right to property). Property is now only a LEGAL right under Article 300A, not a Fundamental Right. The 42nd Amendment (1976, 'mini-Constitution') added Fundamental Duties and expanded DPSP — but it was actually the 44th that corrected several of its excesses and made this specific property change. 61st Amendment lowered the voting age from 21 to 18. 73rd added Panchayati Raj (Part IX).

questions.stem: The doctrine of 'due process of law' was imported into Indian jurisprudence — via a creative reading of Article 21 — in which landmark judgment?

options.option_text: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950)
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)
Keshavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)
Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980)

questions.explanation: A.K. Gopalan (1950) read Article 21 narrowly — 'procedure established by law' meant ANY procedure Parliament laid down, however arbitrary. MANEKA GANDHI (1978) overruled this: 'procedure established by law' now means fair, just, and reasonable procedure — effectively importing American-style 'due process'. It also linked Articles 14-19-21 into the 'golden triangle' — any law restricting personal liberty must pass all three tests simultaneously. Kesavananda is the basic-structure case (Fundamental Rights vs amendment power). Minerva Mills protected basic structure against 42nd Amendment's over-reach.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The Right to Privacy was finally declared a Fundamental Right in K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017). Under which Article(s) does the Supreme Court primarily anchor this right?

options.option_text: Article 21 read with the freedoms under Article 19 and equality under Article 14

questions.explanation: The 9-judge bench in Puttaswamy (24 Aug 2017) unanimously held that the right to privacy is intrinsic to Article 21 (right to life and personal liberty), necessarily linked to Article 19's freedoms, and informed by Article 14's equality principle. The judgment explicitly overruled earlier precedents (M.P. Sharma 1954, Kharak Singh 1962) that had denied privacy as an FR. The 'golden triangle' (Arts 14-19-21) framework — from Maneka Gandhi — was applied here. Note: while the DEFAULT anchor is Article 21, the multi-Article framing in option C captures the complete doctrinal basis.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the six freedoms currently guaranteed under Article 19(1)?

options.option_text: Freedom to assemble peaceably and without arms
Freedom to acquire, hold and dispose of property
Freedom to practise any profession, or to carry on any occupation, trade or business

questions.explanation: The six CURRENT freedoms under Article 19(1): (a) speech and expression, (b) peaceable assembly, (c) form associations/unions, (d) move freely throughout the territory of India, (e) reside and settle in any part of India, (g) practise any profession/occupation/trade/business. Note: 19(1)(f) — the right to acquire/hold/dispose of property — was DELETED by the 44th Amendment 1978 and sub-clause (g) now follows directly after (e). So option C is NOT a current FR (though it was pre-1978).
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Article 20(3) guarantees protection against SELF-INCRIMINATION — 'no person accused of any offence shall be compelled to be a witness against himself'. Which of the following is NOT protected under this provision, as interpreted by the Supreme Court?

options.option_text: Giving oral statements under duress to the police
Giving fingerprints, handwriting samples, or voice samples
Being forced to decrypt a personal mobile-phone passcode
Subjecting the accused to narco-analysis, polygraph, or brain-mapping tests without consent

questions.explanation: In State of Bombay v. Kathi Kalu Oghad (1961), the Supreme Court clarified that Article 20(3) protects against compelled TESTIMONIAL evidence — NOT against the giving of PHYSICAL evidence. Fingerprints, handwriting samples, blood samples, voice samples, specimen signatures etc. are physical/objective evidence and CAN be legally compelled (e.g. under Section 73 of the Evidence Act or Section 311A CrPC). Options A, C, and D are protected: oral statements under coercion (Kartar Singh, Selvi), forced decryption (emerging doctrine), narco/polygraph without consent (Selvi v. Karnataka 2010) all violate 20(3).
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The Right to Education (Article 21A) was inserted into the Constitution by which Amendment Act, and for which age group?
questions.explanation: The 86th Amendment Act 2002 inserted Article 21A — 'The State shall provide free and compulsory education to ALL children of the age of SIX to FOURTEEN years in such manner as the State may, by law, determine.' The enabling legislation is the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act 2009. The 73rd Amendment (1992) dealt with Panchayati Raj, NOT education. The 93rd Amendment (2005) inserted Article 15(5) enabling reservations in educational institutions. The 101st Amendment (2016) introduced GST — unrelated.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Under Article 22(4), a person can be detained under a preventive detention law for more than THREE MONTHS only if:

options.option_text: The Prime Minister personally reviews the case
An Advisory Board — consisting of persons qualified to be High Court judges — has reported sufficient cause for such detention
The President approves the extension under emergency powers

questions.explanation: Article 22(4)(a) specifies that preventive detention beyond THREE MONTHS requires a report from an Advisory Board (members: persons who are, have been, or are qualified to be High Court judges) finding sufficient cause. Alternatively, 22(4)(b) permits longer detention without Board review IF Parliament prescribes it by law (e.g. under the original 1950 Preventive Detention Act). The Advisory Board mechanism is the key procedural safeguard — weakening it undermines preventive-detention accountability. Options A, C, and D invent mechanisms that don't exist in 22(4).
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Which of the following rights has the Supreme Court explicitly READ INTO Article 21 (Right to Life and Personal Liberty)?
questions.explanation: Post-Maneka Gandhi (1978), the Court has expansively read Article 21 to include: right to shelter (Chameli Singh 1995); right to speedy trial (Hussainara Khatoon 1979); right to clean environment (MC Mehta, Rural Litigation & Entitlement Kendra 1985); right to privacy (Puttaswamy 2017); right to livelihood (Olga Tellis 1985); right to health; right to education (Mohini Jain 1992, later codified as 21A); right to die with dignity (Common Cause 2018 on passive euthanasia); right to food; right against sexual harassment at workplace (Vishaka 1997). This expansionist jurisprudence is called the 'golden thread' of Article 21.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Article 20(1) prohibits EX POST FACTO criminal laws. Which of the following falls OUTSIDE the protection of this clause?

options.option_text: Conviction for an act that was not an offence at the time it was committed
Imposing a penalty greater than what was prescribed at the time the act was committed
Imposing a BRAND-NEW retroactive criminal liability on conduct that was previously legal

questions.explanation: Article 20(1) protects against retroactive SUBSTANTIVE criminal law — creating offences or increasing penalties after the act. It does NOT protect against retroactive procedural changes. Courts routinely apply new procedural rules (evidence, trial procedure, sentencing guidelines) to ongoing cases. A classic 2010 Supreme Court case reiterated this: the accused has no right to be tried under the specific procedural law that existed at the moment of the offence. Options A, B, and D are all within the protection. e.g. rules of evidence, trial procedure.
questions.subject: Polity

_fixes.was: Applying a PROCEDURAL change retroactively (e.g. rules of evidence, trial procedure)
_fixes.moved_to_explanation: e.g. rules of evidence, trial procedure

questions.stem: Article 19(2) permits 'reasonable restrictions' on the freedom of speech and expression. Which of the following grounds is NOT enumerated in Article 19(2)?
questions.explanation: Article 19(2) enumerates EIGHT grounds for reasonable restrictions on speech: (1) sovereignty and integrity of India, (2) security of the State, (3) friendly relations with foreign States, (4) public order, (5) decency or morality, (6) contempt of court, (7) defamation, (8) incitement to an offence. 'Scientific accuracy' is NOT among them — and has never been a constitutional ground to restrict speech. The 'sovereignty and integrity' ground was added by the 16th Amendment 1963 in the wake of the China war and secessionist movements.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The safeguards in Article 22 distinguish between 'punitive' and 'preventive' detention. Which of the following safeguards applies to PUNITIVE detention (arrest under ordinary criminal law) but NOT to preventive detention?

options.option_text: Right to be informed of grounds of arrest
Right to be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours

questions.explanation: Article 22(1)-(2) lays safeguards for PUNITIVE (criminal) arrests: right to be informed of grounds of arrest, right to consult a lawyer of one's choice, AND right to be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours (excluding travel time). These do NOT apply to preventive detention — Article 22(3) explicitly excludes preventive detention from 22(1)-(2). Preventive detention gets its own safeguards under 22(4)-(7): Advisory Board for detention beyond 3 months, maximum period fixed by Parliament, grounds to be communicated (but confidential grounds may be withheld in the public interest).
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The 'double jeopardy' clause under Article 20(2) — 'no person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once' — is NARROWER than the American Fifth Amendment version. The key narrowness is that Article 20(2) applies ONLY when:

options.option_text: The previous proceeding was before a competent court AND resulted in either conviction OR acquittal with punishment
Even a mere departmental enquiry has concluded, regardless of outcome
The previous proceeding was only civil in nature
The accused was merely summoned without trial

questions.explanation: Article 20(2) requires BOTH: (i) the earlier proceeding was before a court of competent jurisdiction (quasi-judicial bodies, departmental enquiries don't count); and (ii) the earlier proceeding resulted in conviction AND punishment — a mere acquittal (without the accused having been 'punished') does NOT trigger the bar. Contrast with the US Fifth Amendment which bars RE-TRIAL after acquittal too. The Supreme Court confirmed this narrow reading in Maqbool Hussain v. State of Bombay (1953) — customs confiscation followed by criminal trial was permissible since customs was administrative, not judicial.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Which Article of the Constitution protects a person against the law that makes an act punishable that was legal at the time it was committed?
questions.explanation: Article 20(1): 'No person shall be convicted of any offence except for violation of a law IN FORCE at the time of the commission of the Act charged as an offence, nor be subjected to a penalty greater than that which might have been inflicted under the law in force at the time of the commission of the offence.' This is the ex-post-facto protection. 20(2) is double jeopardy; 21 is life/liberty; 22 deals with arrest/detention. All four articles fall in the same constitutional neighbourhood — hence the common exam trap of confusing them.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Article 19(1)(g) grants the freedom to practise any profession or carry on any occupation, trade, or business. The 'reasonable restrictions' permitted under Article 19(6) include:

options.option_text: Only restrictions imposed in the interest of public order
Prescribing professional/technical qualifications AND carrying on business by the State to the exclusion of citizens
Complete nationalisation of private property without compensation

questions.explanation: Article 19(6) explicitly permits TWO categories of restriction: (i) laws requiring professional or technical qualifications for carrying on an occupation/trade (e.g. Medical Council requirements, Bar Council rules, Chartered Accountant regulations); (ii) laws allowing the State to carry on any trade, business, industry, or service — wholly or partly — TO THE EXCLUSION of citizens (this is the 'State monopoly' provision, used for things like the Indian Posts, certain nationalised industries). Public order is a 19(2) ground for speech restrictions, not a dominant 19(6) ground. Option D would violate Article 300A (right to property as a legal right).
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The Supreme Court in SELVI v. State of Karnataka (2010) ruled that which investigative techniques — when administered WITHOUT consent of the accused — violate Article 20(3) and Article 21?

options.option_text: Interrogation by a magistrate after arrest
Search of personal belongings with a warrant

questions.explanation: In Selvi (2010), a 3-judge bench of the Supreme Court (Balakrishnan CJ, Ganguly, Kapadia JJ) held that INVOLUNTARY administration of narco-analysis, polygraph, and Brain Electrical Activation Profile (BEAP/brain-mapping) tests violates Article 20(3) (self-incrimination), Article 21 (personal liberty, mental privacy), and general standards of 'substantive due process'. HOWEVER, with free and voluntary informed consent, these tests may be used — the RESULTS aren't admissible as direct evidence but may be used for investigation leads. Fingerprinting (option A) is permissible (physical evidence per Kathi Kalu Oghad). Options C and D describe ordinary criminal procedure — unrelated.
